description: We are a team of six students from India. We joined NASA Space Apps Challenge to learn how space data and technology can be turned into something useful, and to build our first project together as a team.
summary:
Orbitwright is an interactive, browser-based space mission design simulator inspired by NASA’s Mission Design Lab and systems engineering workflows. Players take a mission from an initial scientific question through architecture trade studies, spacecraft subsystem configuration, design review, an accelerated 30-day flight simulation, and an engineering debrief.

To address the challenge of making complex mission design accessible and engaging, Orbitwright models real engineering trade-offs across NASA’s four mission segments—Launch, Space, Ground, and User. Every choice in orbit, launch vehicle, power, battery, communications, attitude control, and science instruments updates a live resource ledger and directly determines in-flight vulnerabilities and anomalies. Players can experiment across five distinct science objectives—from Earth storm tracking to lunar ice mapping and Mars mineralogy—either solo or in a four-role local team co-op mode requiring cross-discipline sign-off.
details:
Orbitwright is an interactive, browser-based space mission design simulator inspired by NASA’s Mission Design Lab, Concept Maturity Levels (CML), and systems-engineering workflows.

What It Does & How It Works

Orbitwright guides players through an end-to-end six-stage mission lifecycle across NASA’s four core mission segments—Launch, Space, Ground, and User:

  1. Mission: Players choose from five science objectives (Stormwatch, Near-Earth Watch, Lunar Waterline, Helios Watch, or Red Planet Mapper), set difficulty rules (Sandbox, Cadet, Engineer, or Flight Director), and select either Solo or Team of 4 pass-and-play mode.
  2. Architecture: Players evaluate orbits (LEO, SSO, HEO, GEO, LLO, Mars) and launch vehicles, balancing sunlight intensity, eclipse duration, radiation levels, ground-link quality, and payload mass limits.
  3. Spacecraft: Players configure six subsystems—structure/shielding, solar power, battery storage, communications, onboard computer, and attitude control (ADCS)—alongside up to seven science instruments. A live engineering model updates a real-time resource ledger and SVG spacecraft preview with every change.
  4. Review: An automated design review flags PASS, WARNING, or CRITICAL issues across all four mission segments. In Team mode, all four discipline leads must sign off before launch.
  5. Flight: Players execute an accelerated 30-day operational rehearsal where deterministic in-flight anomalies (solar array degradation, radiation storms, ground-link outages, calibration drift, and unexpected discoveries) are triggered and scaled directly by the spacecraft’s actual design margins.
  6. Debrief: Players receive a weighted final score, a plain-language engineering story explaining why specific bottlenecks or failures occurred, real NASA mission parallels, and a local trade-study leaderboard to compare designs.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Demystifies Systems Engineering: Rather than treating spacecraft components in isolation, Orbitwright makes coupled trade-offs tangible—showing immediately how adding a high-data sensor increases mass, power draw, eclipse battery requirements, and downlink congestion.
  • Accessible STEM Education: Runs directly in any modern desktop or mobile browser with zero installation, progressive plain-language explanations ("Why This Matters"), and multiple difficulty tiers so beginners can explore freely while advanced users wrestle with tight engineering margins.
  • Collaborative Decision-Making: The 4-role local co-op mode (Mission Planner, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, and Flight Operations Officer) mirrors real cross-discipline tension, teaching students and teams how to negotiate compromises between science ambition, reliability, and cost.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

  • Languages & Frameworks: JavaScript (ES2022+), React 18, HTML5, and CSS3.
  • Build & Deployment Tooling: Vite for bundling, Git & GitHub for version control, and Vercel for continuous cloud deployment.
  • Graphics & Persistence: Custom procedural inline SVGs for dynamic spacecraft schematics, orbital diagrams, mission cards, and launch animations, paired with browser localStorage for autosaving designs and trade-study history.
  • NASA & Partner References: Modeled on NASA’s Design and Develop Science Missions four-segment framework, NASA/JPL Concept Maturity Levels, GSFC’s Mission Design Lab, CubeSat 101, and NASA Mission Viz.

Creativity & Key Design Factors Considered

  • Deterministic, Design-Driven Simulation: Instead of arbitrary RNG failures, anomalies are seeded deterministically from the player's architecture so identical spacecraft produce reproducible results—turning failed flights into actionable engineering lessons rather than random luck.
  • Objective-First Scoring: Every instrument earns different science points depending on the chosen mission (for example, a particle detector scores high on Helios Watch but zero on Stormwatch), reinforcing that the "biggest" hardware is useless if it does not serve the scientific question.
  • Playability & Accessibility: Our Team balanced the numerical model across all 15 mission-and-difficulty combinations so multiple distinct architectures (lightweight CubeSat-class builds vs. heavy high-capacity platforms) can succeed, while offering four visual themes (Light, Dark, OLED, and Glass), five accent palettes, keyboard shortcuts, and prefers-reduced-motion support.
